h1: Why bars rinse a glass with cold water before they pour
title: Why bars rinse a glass with cold water | Craft Beer School
desc: That quick upside down rinse at the bar cools the glass, washes away dust and sanitiser and helps the beer pour with a better head.
teaser: The bartender flips your glass onto a little fountain before pouring. Two seconds of cold water make a real difference to your beer.
standfirst: Watch a good craft beer bar and you will see the bartender press each glass onto a small jet of water before it goes under the tap. It looks like theatre. It is one of the most useful two second habits in serving beer.
sections: The gadget on the bar top

The device is called a glass rinser. It sits in the drip tray or on the counter. Press a clean glass upside down onto it and a ring of jets sprays cold water up into the glass for a second or two. Then the glass goes straight under the tap, still wet.

It is not a washer. The glass has already been washed and sanitised. The rinser does a final job that matters a lot in the few seconds between the shelf and the pour. Some bars without one rinse glasses under a cold tap instead, which does the same work less neatly.
It washes off dust and sanitiser

Glasses sit on shelves and in racks, collecting dust between uses. Commercial glass washers also use detergent and sanitiser. A little can remain on the glass after the cycle. Even a trace of either can flatten a beer's head and add a faint chemical note.

A blast of cold, clean water rinses that residue away. It also removes any odour the glass picked up sitting near the kitchen. A busy Indian bar with a tandoor or fryer nearby makes this especially useful, because smoke and oil settle on everything in the room.
It cools the glass without freezing it

A glass straight from a hot glass washer can be at 50 °C or more. Pour a 4 °C lager into that and the beer warms up fast. Warm glass also makes carbon dioxide leave the beer quickly, which means a fobby, foaming pour and wasted beer.

Cold rinse water brings the glass close to tap water temperature in a second or two. That is not frosty, but it is cool enough for the beer to pour cleanly. It is also far better than a frozen glass, which brings its own problems. Our guide on frozen glasses explains why.
A wet glass pours a better head

Beer poured into a dry glass meets a surface full of tiny irregularities that grab bubbles and release gas. A thin film of water smooths that out. The beer slides down the wall instead of churning, so the bartender gets a controlled head of the right size with less overflow.

That is why the rinse happens immediately before the pour. A wet glass left standing for a few minutes picks up dust again and dries unevenly. Good bars rinse, pour and serve in one movement, ideally with a head of about two fingers on most styles.

A mass market lager poured ice cold into a slightly dusty glass will survive. There is little aroma to lose and most drinkers will not notice a thin head. A craft beer bar pouring a fresh pale ale or a wheat beer has more at stake. Customers paying craft beer prices expect a full head, bright aroma and a beer that tastes the way the brewer meant.

That is why the rinser became standard kit in craft bars around the world. It costs little, uses a small amount of water each time and makes every pour more consistent. Some bars set a rule that no glass goes under a tap without a rinse. It is one of the easiest ways to judge a bar quickly: if staff rinse every glass, they probably care about the lines and the cold room as well.

A rinser only works on a glass that is already beer clean. If a glass has a greasy film from poor washing, cold water will not remove it. You will still see bubbles clinging to the sides and the head will still fade fast.

A rinse also does not replace proper glass washing with the right detergent and a good final rinse. Bars that skip the main wash and rely on the rinser are just spreading the problem. If you see a rinser but your beer still has bubbles stuck to the glass, the problem is upstream.

You do not need a rinser at home. Hold a clean glass under a cold tap for a few seconds, let the excess drain for a moment, then pour. If your tap water is heavily chlorinated or tastes of the borewell, use a jug of filtered water instead. The aim is a cool, clean, wet glass with nothing on it except water.

Knowing why each step in a pour matters is the start of tasting beer properly. Once you see how much glass, temperature and foam change what you taste, you start noticing it every time.
Try it with your next two pours

Next time you open two cans of the same beer, pour one into a dry glass and the other into a glass rinsed with cold water. Watch the head and taste both. The difference is small but real. Once you see it you will rinse every time. Our guide on how to pour beer covers the rest of the pour.
faqs: What is a glass rinser at a bar?
It is a small device that sprays cold water up into an upturned glass just before pouring. It rinses off dust and sanitiser and cools the glass.
Does rinsing a glass change how beer tastes?
It can. A rinse removes residue that flattens the head and adds off notes. It also cools a warm glass so the beer stays fresher and pours more cleanly.
Should I rinse my glass at home before pouring beer?
Yes, a quick rinse in cold water just before pouring is a good habit, as long as the glass is already clean.
